newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - CPI, M3 AND CREDIT GROWTH TO SLOW.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - CPI, M3 AND CREDIT GROWTH TO SLOW.

text.p: The market's recent fruitless quest for direction should be satisfied with the release of a batch of South African key economic indicators next week.
First up is March consumer inflation, which will be released on Wednesday at 0900 GMT.
A Reuters consensus poll of 10 economists forecast the overall consumer price index would rise 0.7 percent month-on-month or 9.7 percent year-on-year after a 0.5 and 9.8 percent rise in February.
"The big question is does inflation hit 10 percent or doesn't it," said one economist who asked not to be named.
"You need one percent month-on-month to get 10 percent and I think that is very unlikely because of the slowing effect of interest rates and the appreciating currency," he said.
Official interest rates have held steady since last November, while the rand has strengthened from around 4.70 at the beginning of the year to 4.45 on Friday.
Boland Bank economist Francois Jansen noted, however, that increased taxes on tobacco and alcohol introduced in the budget would also push the month-on-month rate up.
"Usually the increase in 'sin taxes' comes through in March and April," Jansen said, adding that the month-on-month increase over the last four years had been around one percent in March.
The year-on-year figure would be pushed up by the fact that it was coming off a low base a year ago, economists added.
The inflation data will be followed on Friday at 1500 GMT by the Reserve Bank's March money supply and private sector credit extension data.
The consensus called for a 15.04 percent year-on-year rise in money supply growth from a preliminary 15.82 increase in February.
Growth in credit extension was seen rising 16.5 percent from 17.34 percent previously.
"The main contributor to money supply growth will still be credit which will be about four billion rand," said Tertia Jacobs at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak
"But that should be offset to some extent by an decline in net claims on the government," she added.
Economists also cited technical factors -- the year-ago high base -- as one of the reasons why they expected the year-on-year rates to decline.

Jansen noted, however, that a 4.0 percent month-on-month increase in notes and coins in circulation in March, which fed into overall money supply, could result in a month-on-month increase of over two percent which would result in the year-on-year rate being little changed from February.
On credit, economists continued to hold out hope that high interest rates would finally take a bite out of the private sector credit binge.
"We still would expect that high interest rates and indebtedness cause credit to slow," said Rand Merchant Bank Treasury economist Julia Roy.
Economists said there were indications that the consumer credit binge was finally starting to ease and that recent increases appeared to stem from corporate demand.
"The question remains not if but when it starts to turn," one said.
Finally, Customs and Excise has tentatively scheduled March trade data for release towards the end of next week.

Economists who were prepared to stick their necks out on the traditionally volatile figure predicted a surplus of 730 million rand, although the range was a wide 350 million rand deficit to a 1.5 billion rand surplus.
South Africa recorded a trade deficit of 450 million rand in February after a 520 million rand surplus in January.

Economists said there had been suggestions that diamond exports had been excluded from February's figures which could be revised to also include previously undercounted metal and mineral export figures.
